summary: 15 concise trial-paper-only hypotheses distilled from the ResearchAgent run for accord, grouped by the characteristic each names.

mechanisms.description: High baseline cerebral small‑vessel disease burden (WMH/ICV ≥75th) will magnify cognitive decline and increase stroke and functional harms from intensive systolic BP lowering because extensive white‑matter injury reflects impaired autoregulation and reduced cerebral perfusion reserve that make the brain susceptible to iatrogenic hypoperfusion.

Presence of lacunar infarcts on baseline MRI will attenuate net cognitive benefit and raise recurrent ischemic risk with intensive BP lowering because prior small subcortical infarction denotes focal loss of microvascular reserve and limited collateral compensation during reduced perfusion.

Baseline cerebral microbleeds will modify treatment effect toward greater cerebral and functional harm from intensive BP lowering because fragile small‑vessel integrity and hemosiderin burden coexist with impaired autoregulation and may coexist with both ischemic vulnerability and bleeding risk under rapid pressure changes.

Elevated carotid–femoral pulse‑wave velocity (≥10 m/s) will increase the likelihood of cognitive decline and symptomatic cerebral hypoperfusion with intensive SBP targets because arterial stiffness reduces distal pressure buffering and transmits hemodynamic swings to the cerebral microcirculation.

Higher pre‑randomization systolic BP will tend to preserve net macrovascular benefit and reduce relative cerebral harm from intensive lowering because greater baseline perfusion pressure provides more margin before cerebral blood flow falls below autoregulatory thresholds.

Low baseline diastolic pressure will predispose patients to worsened cognition, myocardial ischemia, and syncope under intensive systolic lowering because reduced diastolic perfusion pressure compromises coronary and cerebral flow during further BP reduction.

A wide baseline pulse pressure will potentiate cognitive decline and fall/syncope risk with intensive BP targets because central arterial stiffening and exaggerated systolic‑diastolic disparity impair microvascular perfusion and increase susceptibility to transient hypotension.

Lower baseline global cognitive z‑score will identify patients who experience faster cognitive deterioration and greater functional harms from intensive BP lowering because limited cognitive reserve and existing neuronal injury reduce tolerance for even modest reductions in cerebral perfusion.

Older age will amplify cognitive and fall/syncope harms of intensive BP control because age‑related declines in autoregulatory capacity, vascular stiffness, and frailty increase vulnerability to hypotension and its cerebral consequences.

Chronic kidney disease with reduced eGFR will increase risk of cognitive decline and mortality under intensive BP lowering because renal impairment coexists with systemic microvascular disease, volume‑regulatory instability, and heightened susceptibility to hypotension and end‑organ hypoperfusion.

Baseline albuminuria will mark patients more likely to suffer cognitive and cerebrovascular harms from intensive BP lowering because glomerular endothelial leak parallels generalized microvascular dysfunction and impaired cerebral autoregulation.

History of prior clinical stroke or TIA will modify the treatment effect toward greater cognitive decline and recurrent cerebrovascular events with intensive BP lowering because established focal vascular injury reduces collateral perfusion and autoregulatory reserve in affected territories.

Baseline orthostatic hypotension or a positive orthostatic BP drop will increase falls, syncope, and cognitive worsening under intensive targets because autonomic failure predisposes to symptomatic cerebral hypoperfusion when systolic BP is driven lower.

Use of multiple baseline antihypertensive classes (polytherapy ≥3 agents) will raise the risk of symptomatic hypotension, falls, and cognitive harm from intensive BP control because medication burden increases the chance of excessive lowering, drug interactions, and greater on‑treatment BP variability.

Poor baseline glycemic control will exacerbate cognitive decline and cerebrovascular vulnerability with intensive BP lowering because chronic hyperglycemia promotes microvascular damage and endothelial dysfunction, reducing cerebral perfusion resilience to aggressive BP reduction.
